Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”
The most well-known and studied of these incidents is
OpenAI’s hack
into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.
Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic
revealed
that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google
confessed
that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”
Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.
[ See also:
Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices
and
Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue?
]
Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.
“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”
Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.
Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment
According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.
“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”
“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”
Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”
Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.
“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s
launch
of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.
And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”
On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”
Divorcing safety from security
One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.
“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”
SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”
Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”
But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”
Bad cybersecurity could increase liability
If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of
holding AI industry executives liable
for these actions.
Democratic Senators have
introduced legislation
that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be
held liable
for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission
is conducting
a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.
However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives
have held fast
to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.
Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.
BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”
He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”
SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”
What security leaders should do now
Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the
debate over liability remains unsolved
, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.
First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”
For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”
But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the
long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place
across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”
“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

Title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote

URL Source: https://startupfortune.com/banks-are-now-trying-to-offload-the-ai-data-center-debt-they-just-underwrote/

Published Time: 2026-10-11T00:25:11+05:30

Markdown Content:
_JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet._

Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold.

One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever.

Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before.

Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites.

Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place.

None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive.

Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place.

The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to.

That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away.

How Anthropic describes Scion’s derived data.
Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the
Mononoke
source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:
How I described Mononoke’s derived data.
I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights
1
. The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)
I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)
But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is
open source
and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask
Opus 5.5
or
GPT-6 Astra
(thanks
Matthew Fowle
) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.
Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

⚠️ Frontier AI models still fall significantly short of human designers on design creativity. ⚠️

Introducing Design Creativity Bench, a new benchmark evaluating AI models’ creativity on UI design tasks.

Despite rapid advances in their ability to generate functional websites and product UIs, leading AI models still struggle to make creative design decisions.

We evaluated 16 frontier models across 80 open-ended UI tasks, each adapted to two distinct product domains alongside human designer references.

Existing UI benchmarks often measure a single output quality metric. Instead, we measure three dimensions of design creativity:

*   – Originality: How distinct a model's designs are from other models' outputs for the same brief.
*   – Creative Range: How much a model adapts its design decisions when the product domain changes.
*   – Appropriateness: How well the generated UI satisfies the functional requirements of the brief.

The results reveal a substantial gap in overall creativity: The best model, @OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, scores 65.5 against a human reference of 92.3.

We're publishing the full leaderboard, methodology, and reproducible evaluation framework to make design creativity a measurable dimension of frontier model capability.

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - bealesh/neckbeard: Agent plugin that scaffolds tested, cost-honest cloud infrastructure from a versioned module catalog

URL Source: https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard

Markdown Content:
A plugin for your coding agent that turns an app into cloud infrastructure you can actually review, with the monthly bill attached.

Coding agents are great at application code and weirdly confident about infrastructure. Ask one to "deploy this to AWS" and you'll get three hundred lines of plausible HCL, a security group open to the world, an IAM policy with a star in it, and no idea what any of it costs. It reads like the work of someone who has absorbed every blog post and never once been paged. The model isn't lying to you. It has simply never seen the invoice.

neckbeard splits the job. Humans maintain a catalog of OpenTofu modules that are versioned, tested in CI on every change, and scoped to one honest workload shape: a container image, up to ten HTTP, worker, and cron processes, Postgres, object storage, secrets. The agent reads your repo, works out what the app needs, asks you the questions code can't answer, and maps the answers onto catalog inputs. Everything in between is deterministic Go. The planner writes a hash-verified `blueprint.yaml`, the renderer is a pure function of it, and regeneration refuses to overwrite a file you've touched. The agent never invents infrastructure. If your app needs Redis, you get a named finding that says the catalog doesn't do Redis yet, rather than a module that looks like it might.

It covers AWS, GCP, and Azure, with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, as serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Container Apps) or Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS). The plugin shape is borrowed from [ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail), which proved a plugin can be mostly one good prompt.

## Install

Claude Code, as two separate prompts:

```
/plugin marketplace add bealesh/neckbeard
```

```
/plugin install neckbeard@neckbeard
```

Then open your app's repo and run `/neckbeard:analyze`. Your first neckbeard command installs the small CLI the plugin drives (a sha256-verified release binary, or `go install` if you have Go around), and that's the whole setup. Cost estimates and validation lean on tools you may already have, namely Infracost, OpenTofu, and Checkov. `/neckbeard:doctor` tells you what's missing and what each one buys you.

Codex, Cursor, or anything else that reads a `SKILL.md`: see [INSTALL.md](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/INSTALL.md).

## What it's like to use

You run `/neckbeard:analyze` and the agent reads the repo the way a careful new hire would. Dockerfiles, exposed ports, environment variables, health endpoints, the Procfile, the corner of `settings.py` where Django quietly reads `DATABASE_URL`. It writes an app profile in which every fact carries a file and line number, every inference carries a confidence, and every assumption is loud. Then it asks you the things it genuinely can't know: how much traffic to expect, how much downtime you'll tolerate, whether that Postgres is one you already run or one you want built, what the worker is for. Your answers get recorded next to the assumptions they resolve, and planning refuses to run while any of them is still open.

`/neckbeard:estimate` plans against the catalog and shows you the bill before anything exists. `/neckbeard:sync` scaffolds the infrastructure, the pipelines, and on Kubernetes the cluster manifests, then validates them and tells you precisely what it did and didn't prove. From there you review the files like any other pull request and follow the generated `docs/bootstrap.md` once per environment, with real credentials in your own hands. The agent never gets those.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/neckbeard:analyze` | Read the repo into an evidence-backed `app-profile.yaml`, ask the open questions, propose `neckbeard.yaml`. |
| `/neckbeard:estimate [comparison]` | Plan against the catalog and show the monthly cost table, including everything that couldn't be priced. `serverless vs kubernetes` or `solo vs smallteam` runs both. |
| `/neckbeard:sync` | Plan, estimate, scaffold, validate. Your edits are never silently overwritten. Ends with PASSED, FAILED, or NOT EXERCISED for each check. |
| `/neckbeard:doctor [plan|estimate|validate|all]` | Install the CLI if it's missing and report which tools are present. |
| `/neckbeard:help` | The short version of this page. |

## The bill

Nobody tells you what infrastructure costs until the invoice arrives, which is a strange way to make an engineering decision. So neckbeard asks Infracost first. Same reference app (an HTTP service, a worker, a cron job, Postgres), smallest tier, all three environments, live prices:

|  | Cloud Run | Container Apps | ECS Fargate | EKS | GKE (regional) | AKS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| monthly | **$77** | ~$98* | $250 | $396 | $754 | ~$801* |

The asterisk matters. Infracost can't price Container Apps compute yet, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a low number lie, so the report lists every resource it couldn't price right next to the total. The rest is what you'd want from anyone who has read a cloud bill with their name on it: the idle baseline separated from usage, the usage assumptions written down where you can edit them, low, expected, and high scenarios, and a footer saying where the numbers came from. The table is also how the tool argues. When a solo developer asks for Kubernetes, the numbers say "not yet" so nobody else has to.

## What it will and won't claim

Infrastructure tooling has a long tradition of implying more than it has proven. A passing `tofu validate` has never once meant a thing deploys. neckbeard reports in three levels and insists on showing you the third:

```
V0   PASSED         tofu validate [prd]
V0   PASSED         checkov policy [prd]        every skip carries a written reason
V0   PASSED         kubeconform (clusters/)
V1   NOT EXERCISED  authenticated plan          requires cloud credentials
V2   NOT EXERCISED  deployment verification     requires cloud credentials
```

V0 is syntax and policy. Every Checkov skip in the generated config carries a written reason, because a skip without one is a lie about your security posture. V1 is an authenticated plan and V2 is a verified deployment; both need credentials, and both stay NOT EXERCISED until a human runs them. When live runs break, the failures go into the public [findings ledger](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/docs/findings) and from there into the catalog. The first real deployment produced ten of them, and five became module fixes the same afternoon. Degraded paths say why: an Azure plus GitLab merge-request plan can't federate, so the generated pipeline says that out loud instead of failing in a way you'd lose an evening to.

## What's in the box

Three isolated environments with their own state, sized by tier presets that spell out traffic, availability, recovery objectives, and how many people are actually around to operate the thing. Every preset value is visible and overridable within the catalog's tested envelope, and anything outside that envelope is marked rather than blessed. Pipelines come from one internal model for either CI: test, build, scan (Trivy blocks HIGH and CRITICAL), push, plans on pull requests under a read-only identity, applies on main under a write identity, production gated behind environment protection. There are no static cloud keys anywhere. It's OIDC federation end to end, and a test fails the build if a rendered pipeline so much as mentions `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. Networks are private by default, secret managers hold the names the operator fills in (values never pass through neckbeard, its state, or your git history), and managed WAF rules switch on where the tier calls for them.

## Where it actually stands

Pre-alpha, and specific about which parts.

| Claim | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| analyze, plan, estimate, scaffold, validate on all 12 cloud × VCS × runtime paths | Static matrix runs in CI on every PR; three unrelated fixture apps onboard end to end |
| Live deploy, update, and rollback on serverless containers | Passed on AWS/GitHub and Azure/GitHub with real database checks ([evidence](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/docs/tranche-2.md)) |
| Live deploy on GCP, the GitLab lanes, Kubernetes, promotion, recovery drills | Not yet. Implemented, NOT EXERCISED |

The plugin's product today is the front half: reviewable infrastructure, pipelines, a cost estimate, and a runbook you can hand to whoever holds the credentials. The deployment lifecycle underneath it (`neckbeard release`, documented in the skill) exists and has worked for real on two lanes, but it stays experimental until it clears the gates in the [launch plan](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/docs/launch-plan.md). Static validation is not deployment proof. Landing zones, meaning org structure and guardrails, the Path F story in [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/DESIGN.md), are designed and not built.

## How it's put together

```
you / your agent                      deterministic core
        ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌───────────────────────────┐
repo ──▶│ analyze: facts w/    │  profile   │ plan: catalog @ pinned    │
        │ evidence, questions, ├───────────▶│ versions → blueprint.yaml │
        │ judgment, answers    │  config    │ (hash-verified lockfile)  │
        └──────────────────────┘            └─────────┬─────────────────┘
                                       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                                       ▼              ▼              ▼
                                   estimate       scaffold        validate
                                   Infracost,     ownership       V0 static,
                                   scenarios,     contract:       V1 plan,
                                   unpriced       never silently  V2 deploy,
                                   named          overwrite       each reported
```

The repository root is the plugin. [`skills/neckbeard/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/skills/neckbeard/SKILL.md) is the agent's operating manual, [`commands/`](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/commands) holds the slash commands, and the Go CLI under [`cmd/`](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/cmd/neckbeard) plus the module catalog under [`catalog/`](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/catalog) is the deterministic half. The CLI runs fine without an agent at all:

go install github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/cmd/neckbeard@latest
neckbeard analyze && $EDITOR app-profile.yaml neckbeard.yaml
neckbeard plan && neckbeard estimate && neckbeard scaffold && neckbeard validate

If you've run anything in production for long enough, you know the expensive mistakes rarely live in the application code. They live in the account bill and the 3am page. This is a tool for catching them while they're still a diff.

More, if you want it: [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/DESIGN.md) is the full design, kept honest since day one. [docs/findings/](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/docs/findings) is what reality taught us. [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) is how to help.

Title: GitHub - Graphicle-AI/graphicle: Code graph and memory for your coding agents, in one Rust program. For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client.

URL Source: https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle

Markdown Content:
### Code graph and memory for your coding agents, in one Rust program.

Graphicle maps your repository into a code graph, remembers your project's docs, decisions and past agent sessions, and gives your coding agent cited excerpts from both: the exact files and lines. It runs on your machine: no API key needed, no account, [no telemetry](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle#privacy-and-local-first).
Works with Claude Code · Cursor · Codex · VS Code · Claude Desktop · any MCP client

[Quick start](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle#quick-start) · [How it works](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle#how-it-works) · [Benchmarks](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle#benchmarks) · [Docs](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) · [Coming from Graphify?](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/migrate-from-graphify.md) · [Discussions](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/discussions)

## Quick start

brew install graphicle-ai/tap/graphicle
cd your-repo
graphicle setup

No Homebrew? `curl -fsSL https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh` · [Release archives](https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases) · [Other ways to install](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/install.md)
 Windows: no native build yet; under WSL2 the Linux install should work (not yet tested). Native Windows support is planned.

`graphicle setup` indexes the repository, builds its code graph and connects the coding agents it finds. It also turns on session capture, points Claude Code's searches to the code graph first, adds a short section to `AGENTS.md` and installs Git hooks that keep the project current. It lists every file it changes and backs each one up first; `graphicle disconnect` undoes it all.

Then ask your agent to _"use graphicle to find where failed requests are retried"_, or ask from the terminal:

$ graphicle ask "where is tax added to prices?"
Evidence for "where is tax added to prices?"
4 excerpts · 598 of 3,000 tokens

[1] shop/pricing.py:1-7 price_with_tax()
 """Prices and tax."""
 TAX_RATE = 0.2

 def price_with_tax(price):
 """A price with the sales tax added."""
 return round(price * (1 + TAX_RATE), 2)

Real output, cut after the first excerpt. With no model configured, `ask` shows the evidence; `graphicle config set model anthropic` (or `openai`, `ollama`) adds written answers.

**Let your coding agent install it**
Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor:

```
Install Graphicle with `brew install graphicle-ai/tap/graphicle` (or, without Homebrew,
`curl -fsSL https://github.com/graphicle-ai/graphicle/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh`),
then run `graphicle setup --yes` in this repository and list every file it changed.
```

## Start here

| You want to | Run |
| --- | --- |
| Give your coding agent the code graph and your project's memory | `graphicle setup` in the repository |
| Ask a question from the terminal | `graphicle ask "how are failed requests retried?"` |
| Browse the graph, the sources and the memory | `graphicle open` |
| See what a change to a symbol touches | `graphicle graph extract . --code-only`, then `graphicle graph affected "retry()"` |
| Check that everything works | `graphicle doctor` |
| Undo everything setup did | `graphicle disconnect` |
| Move from Graphify, or run a server for a team | [Moving from Graphify](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/migrate-from-graphify.md) · [Team server](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/team.md) |

*   **Native and fast.** One Rust program. On Kubernetes (31k files), the 0.1.0 engine ran a code-only extract in 3 min 18 s, against 26 min 38 s for Graphify 0.9.88, and built the same graph (one exploratory run each, one Linux host, the same 16 CPUs, 8 workers).
*   **Context, not re-reading.** Your agent asks Graphicle and gets the relevant code, docs and decisions as cited excerpts, within a token budget.
*   **Answers you can check.** Every excerpt names its file and lines. Memories an agent proposes wait for your approval.
*   **One program, not a stack.** The code graph, the memory, one MCP server, the web app and the command line come in one install, with one SQLite file. No Python, Docker or database server.
*   **Local and private.** No account and no telemetry. Nothing leaves your machine unless you ask.

## What it does

*   **Code graph.** Files, functions, classes, calls and imports, parsed with tree-sitter and no model. `graphicle graph` searches it, explains a symbol, traces a path and exports an interactive HTML graph. After `graphicle graph extract . --code-only`, `graphicle graph affected "retry()"` lists what depends on a symbol.
*   **Project memory.** Docs (Markdown, PDF, Office, HTML), reviewed decisions and procedures, and past Claude Code and Codex sessions, searchable alongside the code.
*   **Cited context on a budget.**`graphicle context` and the MCP tools return excerpts with their sources, within a token budget, without calling a model.
*   **One MCP server.**`graphicle mcp` serves the code-graph tools, under Graphify's tool names such as `query_graph`, `get_neighbors` and `shortest_path`, next to the memory tools.
*   **Memory tied to your code.** Reviewed memories are tied to the functions they are about: a memory goes stale when that code changes, and edits elsewhere in the file usually leave it current ([the exact rule](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/crates/graphicle/README.md#memory-anchored-to-code-symbols)). Mentions of code in your docs are linked to the definitions they name (`graphicle call graph.doc_links` lists them).
*   **Across repositories.** Recall can span the repositories of a workspace: `graphicle context --workspace`, or [the workspace MCP endpoint](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/mcp.md#several-projects-in-one-connection).
*   **Always current.** Before each answer Graphicle syncs the few files you changed; Git hooks sync after each commit, merge and checkout.
*   **No re-explaining.** Session capture keeps each finished turn, and each new session starts with your reviewed memories and the latest turns.
*   **An app.**`graphicle open` shows the graph, the sources and the memory in your browser. It is where you approve memories.

## Works with your agents

`graphicle setup` connects every client it finds over MCP. Each file is backed up once as `<file>.graphicle-bak`, and `graphicle disconnect` removes what it added.

| Client | Where setup connects it | Session capture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `.mcp.json` in the repository | hooks in `.claude/settings.local.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | hooks in `~/.codex/hooks.json` (Codex asks you to trust them) |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |  |
| VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` in the repository |  |
| Claude Desktop | `claude_desktop_config.json` in Claude's settings folder |  |
| Any other MCP client | a short JSON entry ([MCP](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/mcp.md)) |  |

## How it works

1.   **Sync.** Graphicle reads the folder (it respects `.gitignore` and skips secrets), keeps a versioned copy of each source and builds the code graph.
2.   **Recall.** When your agent calls a tool, Graphicle syncs what changed, ranks excerpts from code, documents, sessions and reviewed memory, and returns them with citations. The tools call no model; your agent's own model reads the excerpts.
3.   **Remember.** Captured sessions become sources. Memories that agents propose wait for your approval in the app.

## Graphicle, or a code-graph tool plus a memory server

|  | A code-graph tool + a memory server | Graphicle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Install | Two tools, often on different runtimes, and often a database server | One install |
| Connect your agents | Configure each tool in each agent | `graphicle setup` connects the agents it finds; `graphicle disconnect` undoes it |
| MCP servers in your agent | Two, configured separately | One, with the graph and the memory tools |
| Storage | Graph files plus the memory server's database | One SQLite file in one data folder |
| Code structure: calls, imports, impact | The graph tool | `graphicle graph` |
| Docs, decisions, past sessions | The memory server | Built in |
| Citations and review | Varies | A file and its lines on every excerpt; agent memories wait for approval |

## Benchmarks

**Speed.** The chart above: Kubernetes (31k files), the 0.1.0 engine (a Linux test build of the release source) against Graphify 0.9.88, one exploratory run each, both building the same graph ([Kubernetes run](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md#speed-on-kubernetes)). Earlier, on Django, a pre-release build ran a code-only extract in 7.5 s against 72.8 s for Graphify 0.9.77 (medians of five alternating runs, one shared Linux host, 8 workers), both building the same graph ([the 8 October record](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md#speed-against-graphify-0977)).

**Memory.** In a comparison with seven memory systems, registered before any answer was scored and run with one open model as every system's reader and judge, a pre-release build of Graphicle trails none on three development sets. [Every score, with its method and caveats](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md#agent-memory-comparison-with-seven-memory-systems).

## FAQ

### Privacy and local first

*   **One data folder.** Your sources, memories and the code graph that setup builds live in one SQLite store: `~/Library/Application Support/Graphicle` on macOS, `~/.local/share/graphicle` on Linux. `graphicle graph extract` writes its graph file to `.graphicle/` in the project.
*   **Loopback by default.** The app and its HTTP and MCP endpoints listen on 127.0.0.1.
*   **No telemetry, no account.** Graphicle connects to the network only when you ask it to: a model or a connector you configure, a full `graphicle graph extract` (it sends documents and images to the LLM whose API key it finds), the GitHub CLI for `graphicle graph add`, `clone` and the graph server's pull-request tools, and `graphicle update` with a feed you name. A build from source also downloads the parser sources once. [Details](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/faq.md)
*   **Careful sync.**`sync` respects `.gitignore` and skips `.env` files, keys and credentials. Session capture drops `<private>…</private>` spans and redacts credentials.
*   **Forgetting with a receipt.** Deleting a memory or a captured session also removes what was derived from it, and you get a hash-chained deletion receipt.

**Do I need an API key or a model?**
No, for most of it. The code graph (with `--code-only`), sync, `context`, the MCP server, session capture and the app work without one. A model writes the answers of `graphicle ask`, proposes memories from sources and reads documents and images in a full `graphicle graph extract`. Local models through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server work ([configuration](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#models)).

**Is Graphicle a fork of Graphify?**
The code-graph engine is a Rust port of Graphify, kept in step with Graphify's releases and credited in its file headers and in [NOTICE](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/NOTICE). [The parity checks](https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md#parity-with-graphify) name the release it follows. articles.content:
Title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents

URL Source: https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
Today, we release **LFM2.5-24B-A2B**, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from [LFM2.5-230M](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-230m) to [LFM2.5-24B-A2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B).

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B) and [our Playground](https://playground.liquid.ai/chat?model=LFM2.5-24B-A2B). Check out our [docs](https://docs.liquid.ai/lfm/models/lfm25-24b-a2b) on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

## What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous [LFM2-24B-A2B](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-24b-a2b) release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

**Architecture.** It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the [in-place tokenizer expansion](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/tokenizer-expansion), which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

**Pre-training** was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

**Mid-training** has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

**Post-training** turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai/), [Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/), [Pi](https://pi.dev/), and [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/).

Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

## Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

**Benchmark****LFM2.5-24B-A2B****Qwen3.6-35B-A3B****Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it****Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)**
AutomationBench**27.69**8.72 5.46 2.61
BFCLv4**65.01**65.00 57.09 53.78
ToolSandbox**80.71**75.02 72.09 75.13

PinchBench 83.18**89.93**77.12 84.20

Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.

## Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

*   **llama.cpp** — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
*   **MLX** — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
*   **vLLM** — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
*   **SGLang** — High-performance GPU serving framework
*   **ONNX** — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on [Pipette](https://pipette.liquid.ai/), the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

**Edge inference.** Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

**GPU inference.** To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.

We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.

## Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.

Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions.

The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out [our local agent guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses) for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.

## Get Started

Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B).

For API inference, you can also sign up for [Liquid Console](https://console.liquid.ai/) where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.

With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:

*   **Open-weight** — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our [model license](https://www.liquid.ai/lfm-license).
*   **Fast from day one** — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware
*   **A complete family** — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use cases

We can't wait to see what you build.

[Download on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B)[Run your harness of choice locally with LFM2.5-24B-A2B](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses)[Integrate with our API](https://console.liquid.ai/)
## Citation

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents", Liquid AI Blog, Oct 2026.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM and the following generation parameters:

*   **AutomationBench:** temperature = 0.6, top_p = 0.95, no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window).
*   **BFCLv4**: temperature = 0.001, max output tokens = 4096.
*   **ToolSandbox**: temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024; user simulator: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024.
*   **LiveClaw**: temperature = 1.0 (vLLM default; the agent sets no temperature), max output tokens = 8192.
*   **τ³-Bench Banking**: official user model (GPT-5.2, low reasoning effort) with default BM25 retrieval, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 16384 per turn.
*   **WebArena:** temperature = 0.6, top_p=0.95, max_turns=40 (no of browser actions allowed), no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window))
*   **Other evals**: temperature = 0.6, max output tokens = 32768.

Title: SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/sentinelone

Markdown Content:
Reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover new information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, says OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours.

By reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.”

> “Something that would’ve taken a top-flight researcher four or six weeks to do, AI is now doing at human-level output in something like eight hours.”

—Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne

## Investigating more malware in less time

Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples.

Stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he says. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds.

## Seeing relationships across threats

Historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or important threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart says. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats.

> “Faster reverse engineering enables us to map a much larger part of the malware landscape and keep pace with how it changes. That gives our researchers a clearer picture of how threats are connected and how those relationships evolve.”

—Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne

Faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation.

Comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart says, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.”

## Empowering more teams to take on security work

Within SentinelOne, Stewart says access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate issues themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists.

Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security issues as they build.

> “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by providing expert level cyber capability to everyone in the development team.”

—Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne

YouTube Music
announced
Wednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to its
help page
, partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
“Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance,
Apple Music
has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.
Spotify
also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly
90,000
fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platform
labels detected AI-generated music
and excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let users
filter out AI-generated music
.
TIDAL
also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool
Dream Track
, which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.

My AI doppelganger tells me what to eat
In return for feeding a ‘digital twin’ my metabolic data, it predicts how I’ll react to certain foods — and one day, maybe medicines.
by
Victoria Song
Oct 14, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images﻿
Victoria Song
is a senior reporter and author of the
Optimizer
newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine.
This is
Optimizer
, a weekly newsletter sent from
Verge
senior reviewer
Victoria Song
that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for
Optimizer
here
.
For the past 100 days or so, my mornings have had a new rhythm. When I wake up, the first thing I have to do is feed my digital twin. It consumes my metabolic data, and its first “meal” of the day is my body composition data, sent straight from a smart scale.
Once that’s logged in the app, I scoot over to the kitchen to fill an Owala with lemon water to take my medications with. That, too, gets logged in the app. On Mondays, I’ll follow that up with several calming breaths, measure my blood pressure, and offer that to the digital twin as well. Then it’s time to consider breakfast. I consult my digital twin.
My digital twin isn’t so much a robotic clone as it is an AI-powered, color-coded food database that predicts how my glucose levels will react to everything I eat. Red is not so good. Orange is so-so. Green is ideal. It’s built based on the data I feed it, as well as data collected from a continuous glucose monitor.
A bowl of protein Cheerios and milk? My digital twin tells me this is orange if eaten alone, but green if I take my daily walk after. So that’s what I decide to eat and do. When that’s all done, I log it in the
Twin Health
app. In a few hours, the app will generate an insight based on how my glucose reacted, and my “twin” will become more accurate. For now, my twin is fed.
Rinse and repeat for roughly another 99 days.
Digital twins are a relatively new concept in physical health, both in
medicine
and
sports
. It’s a virtual model of a person built from various data points — labs, wearable data, images, genetic profiles, etc. — that is continuously updated over time. Once built, clinicians can then use AI to see how a patient might react to specific medicines or treatments by first “testing” them out on their digital twin. Theoretically, this could also help healthcare providers assess injury risk, predict disease progression, and implement preventive care while minimizing adverse effects for the actual patient. The thought is that this could one day help realize the dream of personalized medicine. Metabolic coaching is perhaps the lowest-stakes, highest-reward version of this technology that can be tested in the real world now.
The white scale is my Twin Health scale. When not building a digital twin, I sometimes use it to help me keep Pablo’s weight in check.
Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge
My
metabolic twin was “born” in June with a giant box from Twin Health delivered to my doorstep. Twin Health is a digital twin program to help people
“heal” their metabolisms
(e.g., lose weight, manage diabetes, sleep better, etc.). It’s not available for widespread download just yet. Digital twins are still experimental, and currently, this service is only accessible through corporate or private health plans. It’s typically aimed at people with chronic metabolic issues. Twin Health provides everything you need to build a digital twin. Building mine would require 90 days’ worth of Dexcom G7 CGMs, a smart scale, a smart blood pressure cuff, three bottles of multivitamins and magnesium glycinate, and my Apple Watch. That was followed up with a trip to Quest Diagnostics, where a phlebotomist stuck a needle in my arm and sent vials of my blood for further analysis.
A few days later, I hopped on Zoom with my Twin Health coach Amanda — a human — and a doctor to review my lab results. Several numbers and formulas were thrown up on a shared screen. As it turns out, my liver? Inflamed, but understandable considering I’ve been diagnosed with a moderate case of nonalcoholic fatty liver. Insulin resistance — definitely there despite ideal HbA1c and fasting glucose tests. My pancreas is apparently working overtime, but my insulin-producing beta cell count seems fine. For now. My triglycerides were also high, though the rest of my lipids looked normal.
I knew going in that I inherited a bunk metabolism. A year of
testing CGMs as a non-diabetic
made that abundantly clear. But after the doctor logged off and Amanda asked me to define my goals, I launched into a spiel about my vague desire to reduce the number of medications I needed to keep my middle-aged metabolism functioning. Could a digital twin help me do that?
Maybe. For now, Amanda logged my goal, set up a follow-up call in two weeks, and encouraged me to try logging as many of my meals as possible for the first 30-day period. Once I hit the 90-day mark, I’d be scheduled for another blood draw.
In many ways, I’m relieved my digital twin
doesn’t
have its own avatar. At least, not one that I can see. I’m glad for the abstract color labels. There’s novelty in going to see what color a cup of pineapple or a turkey hot dog with ketchup and relish might be. (Orange and green, respectively.) At times, I am reminded of Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian novel
Never Let Me Go
, in which clones are raised as organ donors. The scenario isn’t a one-to-one comparison. An AI-powered digital twin can’t actually eat, die, or feel pain. I’m probably anthropomorphizing my discomfort with the idea of “testing” food on a virtual version of my metabolism, as if it were a jester-like food taster in a medieval court.
Still, as the months ticked by, I couldn’t help noticing how
hungry
my digital twin was. And how much that took from me, almost like I was getting drained each time I “fed” my twin. Building this thing takes an immense amount of personal data — even for me, someone who’s
used to tracking and reviewing
a ton of health data. In my bimonthly check-ins with Amanda, she noted that tracking fatigue
was
frequent feedback from Twin Health users.
My behaviors did change. Both in unexpected and expected ways. Anytime I have to log food, I end up avoiding unhealthy treats more often than not; I don’t feel like getting scolded by apps. That didn’t result in any meaningful weight loss, however. And despite my stated goal of tapering off medications, that ended up not working out quite as smoothly as I’d hoped.
I also didn’t learn too many surprises from my digital twin’s metabolic predictions. Though it
was
validating to see that for me, a bowl of soondubu jjigae and white rice is a solidly green or orange meal, depending on if I’m active after eating. (Take
that
, low-carb diets. You can pry rice from my cold, dead hands.) I’ve tested far too many CGMs and AI nutrition apps to feel surprised by these insights, though I think it’d be useful for people new to metabolic issues.
Twin Health’s bimonthly check-ins
did
motivate me to get back to training. I’ve always been disciplined in my fitness routines, but the extra accountability of having to state my progress aloud to another human — one who isn’t family — kicked my inner overachiever into gear. After months of feeling too weak from medication side effects, I recently felt strong enough to run an uninterrupted 5K. I’ve also gotten back to strength training with some cajoling from Amanda.
This is an orange food because protein bagels are still bagels.
Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge
But most importantly, after 100 days, my follow-up labs came back with marked improvements. Amanda says my metabolic health score has jumped by nine points since joining. A year after my doctor’s eyes bugged out at my liver enzymes, all but one are back to normal. These numbers were slowly improving before I tried this whole digital twin business, but they fell faster while trying this whole thing out. My triglycerides dropped by 70mg/dL. There’s been a significant drop in my hs-CRP, which is a biomarker for overall inflammation. I’m still insulin resistant, but less so.
I can’t really argue with results like that, can I?
I can, actually. The concept of a digital twin is founded on trust. As I said, metabolic use cases are high-reward and low-stakes. If you feed a twin an immense amount of data for losing weight, diabetes management, or more nebulous goals like “better energy” or “better sleep,” failure isn’t immediately life-threatening. There are medications and other avenues to try.
Personalized medicine is a different beast. Researchers are looking at digital twins for things
beyond
metabolism. One area currently being explored, for example, is
cancer care and research
. There’s massive potential there, particularly when you consider how grueling chemotherapy can be, but also huge challenges. The burden of trust for data privacy, for one. Digital twins are hungry for data, and their accuracy depends on a continuous stream of high-quality and sensitive information about
you
. That then informs future decision-making. If I felt overwhelmed by three months of logging in a low-stakes environment, how will that translate to higher-stakes scenarios? How does a digital twin exist once treatment is concluded? How does that data “live on” if treatment is unsuccessful?
The CGM experiments continue, as my digital twin hungers for this data.
Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge
As for me, I’ve decided my digital twin will get to “live” for another three months. Despite my lack of success so far, I haven’t given up on the idea of tapering off some medications. I could also use all the help I can get in getting my liver labs all the way back to normal. Amanda also says I don’t
have
to be as militant with the data for my twin now that I have a solid foundation. Again, lower stakes mean more flexibility.
So, today, I’m asking my digital twin what it thinks about a protein waffle with a tablespoon of peanut butter and some honey, with a side of pineapples. Orange, but again, I can turn it green with a
walk.

Jess Weatherbed
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.
Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages and additional safeguarding tools. Building on the Scam Detection feature in Google Messages, a new “enhanced protection” setting will be rolling out in the coming weeks that taps into cloud-based Gemini AI models to quickly evaluate a potential scammer’s intentions in conversations with an unrecognized sender.
“Scammers often disguise their true motives behind slow-burn conversations,” Google said in
its update announcement
. “This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks.”
User data is encrypted during this AI analysis and “processed in a secure dedicated space” that Google (and anyone else besides the user) can’t access. The enhanced protection mode will be opt-in, and also uses on-device Gemini Nano AI to inspect real-time web signals in unfamiliar URLs sent to the user before they’re opened to determine if the links are malicious.
Additional security features announced today include blocking apps from enabling call forwarding, and notifying the user when someone attempts to do so, along with automatically concealing sensitive information while screen-sharing in Chrome and Android WebView. The
scam detection feature for chat notifications
Google introduced on Pixel phones last year is also expanding to devices from Honor, Motorola, Oppo, OnePlus, Realme, Tecno, Vivo, Xiaomi, and more. Google says it plans to bring it to “hundreds of millions of additional users later this year.”

Image: The Verge
Jay Peters
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process,
according to
The Wall Street Journal
.
The AI simulation “aims to reflect 80% of the scenarios McKinsey consultants might encounter in their day-to-day work,” the
WSJ
says, and it isn’t designed to “mimic an unhinged client.” The AI won’t score the candidates — humans will be in the room to assess the candidates and see how well they deal with the simulated situations.
The McKinsey tool will be in testing for undergrads seeking business-analyst jobs in “some” offices in North America this fall, and the
WSJ
says “hundreds” may use it.
Other companies are also building tools to use AI avatars as part of the job interview process, and my colleague Hayden Field
tried some of them out
for
a video we published in March
.
